edges.effect_quant: Meta-analyses consistently report shorter hospital stays with earlier postoperative mobilization, with reductions on the order of roughly 2 days in emergency and gastrointestinal surgery syntheses.
edges.mechanism: Early mobilization can counter postoperative deconditioning, improve pulmonary mechanics, and speed gastrointestinal recovery, all of which can move discharge readiness earlier. The effect is usually strongest when mobilization is embedded in a broader enhanced-recovery pathway rather than treated as an isolated event.
edges.summary: The clearest current message is that earlier mobilization after surgery tends to shorten hospital stay, especially within enhanced-recovery pathways. The most recent emergency-surgery meta-analysis and the gastrointestinal-surgery synthesis both point in that direction, and older ERAS colorectal data support the same operational conclusion even though those pathways include more than mobilization alone.
edges.caveats: Mobilization is often studied as one component of an ERAS bundle, so it is not always possible to isolate its independent contribution precisely. Benefits also vary by surgical population, protocol intensity, and baseline illness severity, which keeps this edge supportive rather than definitive.
